segments.text: OK, so I'm going to read you some of this story, OK John? It was eerily quiet, save for some splashing from the sea lion pool. Quote, "It was like there was this [BLEEP] mist," Davilla said, speaking slowly and dramatically. "And the bird was there." You took the bird out of its cage, you said. The bird looked at you. Quote, "I said wow, what are you looking at man? Come on man, let's go. And we went."

segments.speaker: John Bryant      Davilla
segments.text: Yeah, that was a dream I had the day after the party. And I remember that dream. And I remember thinking that I gotta stop smoking pot, man.

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: I'm awfully disappointed, John.

segments.speaker: John   Bryant   Davilla
segments.text: What did you expect?

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: I don't know.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: What did you expect?

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: I thought there was a point.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: Eric is very disappointed here.

segments.speaker: Eric  Holm
segments.text: I feel cheated, man.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: Well did you think he really had the conversation with the Bird?

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: No, but I thought he thought he did.

segments.speaker: John Bryant Davilla
segments.text: I think I did, actually, to be honest with you.

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: No, come on Johnny, you're just telling us what we want to hear.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: You're making stuff up.

segments.speaker: John Bryant Davilla
segments.text: No, it's a true story, man. And when they ask you, you say it's a true story.

segments.speaker: Ira   Glass
segments.text: So the version of the story that they have always told, that they have wondered if it's true, that's the version of the story they're going to have live with. Because nobody, nobody in this world besides them has cared enough about this story to remember it. The facts will stay forever unconfirmable.

segments.speaker: Ira   Glass
segments.text: And when I ask Eric and Alex why this story has stuck with them, and why they've been retelling this story for years, long after they went on to become real reporters for real newspapers, this story is still their favorite story? They truthfully do not have much of an answer. Mostly they say, they just liked everybody who they interviewed for this story. Everybody told them such amazing things. And yes, this is a story about a crime. And yes, the parrot dies. But nobody is really out to hurt anybody in this story or do any harm, including Johnny.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: There is a sort of innocence. He wasn't out to make money off the thing. He didn't want to kill it. He loved it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think the parrot made everybody in this story take leave of their senses including the two of you.

segments.speaker: Eric  Holm
segments.text: I think that that has never crossed my mind before today, but I think you might be absolutely right on that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like look at this. Everybody's going out of their way for the parrot. He takes the parrot for no good reason. The next two people take the parrot really for reasons that make no sense at all. They take a parrot to distract a woman from talking to her husband, or boyfriend, whatever. And then the two of you, for no reason at all, you're never going to make money, you're never going to write a story. Just keep reporting this story for months for no one.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: It makes no sense, our behavior. And we wouldn't have done it if it had been a kitten.

segments.speaker: Ira   Glass
segments.text: I don't know man, a kitten?

segments.speaker: Eric    Holm
segments.text: When we tell the story over and over, by the way, a lot of people, they think there's a punch line at the end.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: And there's never a punch line.

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: The story just sort of peters out.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: Well, not necessarily.

segments.speaker: Ira  Glass
segments.text: Maybe you need a punchline. You need a punchline.

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: We actually got some suggestions last night.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: From the movie star, he sort of suggested a punchline.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Who was the movie star?

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: Topher Grace, the guy from That '70s Show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, and Topher Grace had the suggestion for the ending?

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: He did, he had an excellent suggestion.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: The scene is the apartment, the police barge in--

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: Dawn is on the floor with a jackboot on her neck. And the cops haul everyone away--

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: There's one detective who's sort of--

segments.speaker: Eric Holm
segments.text: --left alone in the apartment.

segments.speaker: Alex Lane
segments.text: He's the one charged with taking the bird, taking possession of the bird. So he opens the cage. And he looks at the parrot, and he says, "You want to go? " And the parrot says, "Yeah." And he says, "Let's go."

segments.speaker: Eric  Holm
segments.text: And, scene.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alex Lane is a staff writer for the Star Ledger in Newark. Eric Holm just started at Bloomberg News. In those jobs, they both do factual reporting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, so two pigs, a parrot, a Jew, a Canadian, and David Sedaris walk into the second half of the show. And the first pig says to the second pig, is it me or do these coming-up-next announcements just keep getting longer? More in a minute from Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose some theme, bring you a variety of different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show, the parrot and the pot-bellied pig. Stories where these two humble animals are just trying to lead their animal lives and simply by being alive they create all kinds of havoc around them, without ever intending to.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We've arrived at Act Two of our show, Act Two, Pig. Well, one of our regular contributors here on This American Life, Jonathan Goldstein has been hosting a new radio show on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation called Wiretap. And he has this story of people and animals.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: The other day, my friend Tony called me up and told me he had the funniest story for the radio. All he'd say was that involved him, his ex-girlfriend, and a road trip they made with a pot-bellied pig. Before Tony would tell me anything further, he said he wanted me to be running a tape recorder. This way, he said, when it played on the radio there'd be my surprised laughter egging him on.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: But here's the thing. I hardly ever laugh. If there's one thing I could change about myself, it would be that. Working in radio, I wish I had the kind of free and easy laugh that felt like an arm around the shoulder. A laugh that said, speak on you darling clown, I am so with you. Instead, I produce silences that, rather than encourage, make a storyteller feel like they're being scrutinized. Or worse, like I just put the phone down to go out and put more change in the parking meter.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: So Tony started telling me the story, and, as usual, I wasn't laughing. But I started to realize that this time was different. For once, I wasn't laughing because the story wasn't funny. But any way, I'm getting ahead of myself. I'll let Tony tell the story.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I guess it kind of marked, pretty much, the end of my relationship with Susan, my last girlfriend. We'd been going out for about four years, and the relationship was on its last legs and had been for, pretty much, about a year.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: Susan is an animal enthusiast, lover. She is always trying to save something. She's always online looking for rescue animals that she obviously, she can't possibly rescue any of them, actually. Or maybe one or two, but she's obsessed with it.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And there was a couple that we knew that about a year ago or a year and a half ago, they got a pot-bellied pig, a baby pot-bellied pig.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: Are they farmers?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: No. They're just like regular city folk. One of them had a head shop-- just like scenesters. And I guess, like my first reaction was that's kind of, I don't know, that's kind of stupid. You don't bring a pig home to the city, to a house. It just seemed like kind of a scenester thing to do like, hey, the guy got a pig.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: But, so they got a pig. And it was really cute. And they showed me pictures and convinced me that it was pretty smart and fun. And it was OK running around the house and in their yard, and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: What was the pig's name?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: Pig's name was Warren. Nothing was heard from the pig or the couple for a while. And then there were some rumblings. I started talking to them. And well, it's not going so well. You know he's ruining the place, and he's out of control and all this stuff.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And before long, Susan was on the case to make sure that he found a good home and happy life. She called around and found a place, an animal sanctuary, outside of Montreal. And they were like, yes, of course bring the pig. And so Susan made arrangements to bring the pig there.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I know what's about to happen, and I don't want to have anything to do with it. And, of course, I'm approached to do the job, to drive this pig to Montreal.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: In your car.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: In my car. And I know, I know at this point in my heart, in my gut, that I'm going to be doing this, because you can't get in Susan's way when she's trying to save an animal. She's unstoppable. And in my mind, it was very clear. Drive with pig to Montreal or deal with the repercussions of not doing that for about a week.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Give me a sense of how big this pig is, like, how much does it weigh?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: 250 pounds? It's a pot-bellied pig. It's not like a big-ass, sort of, regular pork pig. He was just kind of like a children's book pig. And hairy-- pot-bellied pigs they have fur.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Are they pink?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: No, they're kind of brown. So OK, let's put the pig in the cage and let's go do it. And within a couple of minutes realized the cage is not going to fit in my car. There's no way. So like OK, well, we'll just put the pig in. We'll cover the back seat with garbage bags and whatever, and it'll be fine. And at that point, I'm just not thinking. I want to just get this over with. Let's just get the pig in the car. Let's drive. Let's go.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: But we did. We covered the back seat and we started to drive. The first 20 minutes we're kind of all right. The pig was hanging out in the back. Susan was feeding him and petting him. And everything was fine.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: Then about-- probably about 45 minutes into it, the pig started to get more and more agitated. We ran out of food. We had to stop and get some more food. We got like a big bag of bird seed and just a couple of other varieties of dog biscuits and whatever. We stopped at places. They didn't have pig food per se, because people don't usually keep pigs.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: We're driving, and I'm starting to realize that, we're both starting to realize that Warren, the pig, is getting more and more agitated. Like he's not happy. He is getting really restless. He's becoming less and less interested in the food. He is getting more and more persistent about getting up to the front seat. At this point, I can sense the pig's head popping over my right shoulder, sort of snapping. And trying to get over to my left shoulder with the window, and then back over my right shoulder and snapping. And soon had a full body hold on it, trying to keep it away from me.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And this sort of thing really started to turn into something else. I mean, you're in a situation like that with somebody, I suppose the kind of mature, adult, useful thing to do would be to accept the you're in a situation. But I was not happy. I let it be known.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And most importantly, and most significantly for Susan, I was not laughing. Because after a certain point, she started to find it funny, like most people do. Most people start to find story funny around this point, even sooner. I didn't find it funny at all.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: The more she laughed, the more funny she found it, the more upset and angry I got. So she had the pig to deal with, and then, I guess, she had me to deal with. Finally, I came up with the idea that what we needed was a barricade to put between us and the pig, to keep it the pig in the backseat, to keep us from getting hurt. Whatever happened to the back of the car happened at this point because we're in survival mode.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: We're driving around behind strip malls looking for a big piece of cardboard. Finally, we found what looked like something that a refrigerator been in. And I grabbed it. It was soaked in garbage, and it was raining that day. And I opened the car door. Susan is holding the pig back with all her strength. And I jammed this big piece of cardboard, slid it in like when magicians-- when they cut people in half, just slid it into the car, with all my strength, as far as it could go. And I closed the door.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And it worked. And the funny thing is, he didn't even fight. As soon as the barricade went up, he just gave up. We drove the rest of the way to the farm and cut him loose. And he joined his brothers and sisters, his new brothers and sisters, which were these gigantic, fat pot-bellied pigs. Which, I guess, in a short time he'd be like them.

segments.speaker: Jonathan  Goldstein
segments.text: And was that, I mean was that like a beautiful moment?

segments.speaker: Tony  Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I wouldn't say it was beautiful. I felt relieved that the pig was out of my car. And we broke up within a month of this incident.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Do you think that this was the straw that broke the camel's back for Susan?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: She actually said as much. She just said, I can't be with somebody who can't find the humor in the moment in something like that, no matter how dangerous it is, no matter how stupid or crazy, or wrong it is. That's not how I want to live my life.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And when he told you that, did you feel like, I could change?

segments.speaker: Tony  Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I wanted to change, but I could not possibly enjoy life as much as she does. I think she had a point. And I think she was right about me getting too upset over that and not seeing the humor in it.

segments.speaker: Tony  Asimakopoulos
segments.text: The thing about me and Susan-- Susan loves it when things go wrong, because that's when the real fun begins. That's when the real wackiness and zaniness, and the hilarity ensues. And she just thrives on that. She just loves it.

segments.speaker: Tony  Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I don't. I don't. I like it when things go right. I like things to be relatively under control. And the thing I resented about Susan was that she was constantly trying to pull me into her sort of way of having fun. In a sense, Susan was trying to help me have some fun. There's no question in my mind that the way that I react to situations that I'm unhappy with, unhappy to be in, disapprove of, is really, really similar to the way my father used to react to me all the time.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Like, how do you mean?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: Well, kind of stern, disapproving, punitive, making you feel stupid, making you feel like you're doing stuff wrong. I think the defining moment between me and my father was Halloween. I think I was nine. And I went to my friend Sunny's house, he lived down the street, and he had a makeup kit. And he made me up. I don't know. I guess it was some combo of drag and weird clown thing, and zombie. I don't know. We just made it up.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: He made me all up, and I put on a dress. And I ran out into the street and started knocking on everybody's door and just like, I don't know, just yelling and screaming and being an idiot. Just like I'm going to cross from blah, blah, blah running down the street, and, before I knew it, I was at my door.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: And knocked on the door, and I was so out of control at that point. I didn't give a [BLEEP]. I didn't care about anything. I didn't care that I was knocking on my door. My father answered the door. And like a moment of shock. And he grabbed me and pulled me in and started smacking me. Because I was embarrassing him. Because I was doing something completely stupid and embarrassing and having fun.

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: If you try to control everything and OK, this is going to work like that. Well you break up with people. If a best friend is too much of a hassle, just crazy at text, and three hours on the phone every two days, blah, blah, blah. After a while, you cut everything out of your life. And then you get lonely and bored. And I have fewer and fewer stories to tell. And I mean, what do you do when you don't have enough stories to tell, is you go looking for trouble.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: How so?

segments.speaker: Tony      Asimakopoulos
segments.text: Well, I'm just like wandering around at night, walking by bars, looking for people to pick fights with, just somebody that will annoy me or irritate me. He looks good, I'm going to hang around and see what he's saying. It's a bringing to bear my frustration onto an outside thing that deserves to have my fury unleashed upon it.

segments.speaker: Jonathan       Goldstein
segments.text: Do you miss Susan?

segments.speaker: Tony   Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I do. I miss her because I was close to her, and I love her, and I think she's a wonderful person. I love the way she dealt with people. And I loved the way she was. And I wanted to absorb some of that. I wanted some of that to rub off on me. I want some of that.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And did you get it?

segments.speaker: Tony Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I have some of that.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: What do you think that she saw in you that was alluring to her?

segments.speaker: Tony        Asimakopoulos
segments.text: I don't know. I don't know. Maybe I was another animal for her to save.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jonathan Goldstein's CBC radio show Wiretap is at www.cdc.ca/Wiretap. Thanks also to his friend Tony Asimakopoulos and to Sarah Gilbert.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, Combo Platter. Starting out today we have had a story about a parrot, and we've had a story about a pig. And to end today's show, we have this story from David Sedaris.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: When asked why she'd chosen to become a journalist, the parrot was known to cock her head a half an inch to the right, and pause for a moment before repeating the question. "Why did I choose to become a journalist? Well, I guess what really drives me is the money-- that and the free booze." It killed her to follow this with, "I was just joking about the money."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The paper she worked at was called The Eagle. And she wrote for the Tempo section, which was later renamed Lifestyles, and was now titled, simply, Living. Most of her stories were little more than puff-pieces. Interview the wealthy tortoise who'd shelled out money for the new speedway. Cover the benefit gala for ringworm, or heartworm or the earthworm or anti-defamation league.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: She wanted an opportunity to show her chops and finally got her break when a pot-bellied pig took over as director of the local art museum. The Eagle wanted something simple, 300 words tops, but the parrot thought differently. It scheduled a long lunch. Her guest arrived on time, and after ordering they got down to business.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "So," the parrot began, "it's a long way from Ho Chi Minh City to the much coveted director's chair of a noted museum. I'd like you to reminisce about the journey a little."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "I'm sorry," the pig said. "But I've never been to Ho Chi Minh City."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "But you are from that region are you not?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "No," the pig told her, not at all.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The parrot ran her fat, black tongue over the ragged edge of her upper beak. "I don't mean to contradict you," she said, "but I have done a little leg work, and it seems that you're officially registered with your health care provider as a Vietnamese pot-bellied pig. So let's turn our thoughts eastward, shall we, and talk about your past."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Technically, yes, I am a Vietnamese pot-bellied pig," the museum director said. "But that's just a silly formality. The fact is that I was born in this country, as were my parents and their parents before them."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "I see," the parrot said. And she scratched the words self-hating onto her notepad. "So how will your ethnicity reflect itself in regards to our museum? Can we expect to see more Oriental art, a pricey new Ming wing, perhaps some big Treasures of The Emperor extravaganza?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Nothing's planned," the pig said.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "But you wouldn't rule it out?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Well, no, not completely, but--"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "That's all I wanted to know," the parrot said. And at that moment, their lunch all arrived.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: It was she who had made the reservation, and, in a moment of inspiration, she decided they'd go to Old Saigon. The fact that it was her idea would not be mentioned in the article. Nor would she add that the pig had never in his life used a pair of chopsticks, and that he gripped them, one in each hoof, as if they were screwdrivers.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: During the meal, a few blades of lemongrass for him, a Mekong platter for her. They talked about this and that, but she wasn't really engaged, busy as she was dreaming up a headline. Museum Takes on Asian a Slant was good, but she'd have to fight hard to get it past her editor who despised, what she called, word play.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: When their lunch was over, the pig trotted back to the museum, and the parrot headed down to the VFW Hall, where she hoped to round out her article. There she spoke to a red-shouldered hawk, who hadn't actually fought in Vietnam but might have had the war lasted just a few weeks longer.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "I could have practically been killed over there, and now one of them is coming to my museum trying to tell me what art I should look at?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "I know it," the parrot said.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The article was due the following morning, and she stayed up all night in order to finish it. Her editor scowled at the bulk of pages but softened after the first read through saying, " Good work, you," and, "Maybe we should send this over to the city desk."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The eventual headline was no masterpiece, Pot-bellied Museum Director Stirs Controversy. But the parrot was so relieved to move out of the Living section that they could have called it Mud and she wouldn't have cared. As for the pig, he wasn't nearly as upset as she thought he would be. Rather than threatening a lawsuit or demanding a retraction, he phoned to say that he was disappointed. "Deeply disappointed," were his exact words.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The parrot reached for a pen, hoping for quotes that might lead to a second article. "Is that all you have to say?" she asked.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Any response," he sighed. And gently hung up the phone.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Hello," the parrot said, "Hello."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The pig would not have admitted it, but what really bothered him was the pot-belly business. He'd been plump all through his youth, and the years of name calling had not just shaped his adult life but deformed it, like some cell made crazy by radiation.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: He couldn't remember the last time he'd eaten without thinking. Popped a passing canape into his mouth, finished an entire potato chip or dry roasted peanut without calculating the damage. While others prepared for bed, he ran a treadmill. They tucked into their ample breakfasts, and he hung upside down from a bar in his living room, doubling at the waist until he saw stars. Then came the traditional sit-ups, and a half a slice of dry Ry-Vita before examining his silhouette in the hallway mirror and getting ready for work.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: He did not have a pot-belly. He would never again have a pot-belly. But now, here was this article, essentially, comparing him to Buddha. After hanging up on the reporter, the pig began a three-day fast. Lunchtime came, and as his colleagues shuffled to the museum cafeteria, he sat at his desk and looked out the window at that stupid hawk, marching back and forth with his picket sign.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The veteran had hoped that others might join him, but none of his fellows seemed to care. "The war is over, and it's time to move on," they'd been quoted as saying. "Who cares if some," and there was that word again, "Who cares if some pot-bellied Charlie wants to hang a picture on the wall?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Damn that parrot from the Eagle." The pig's anger felt vaguely nourishing, but he knew that it was misplaced. The reporter hadn't assigned the animals their names. That was someone else's doing, someone who sat back and ordained, wide-mouth bass, humpback whale, lesser wart-nosed horseshoe bat, not caring whose life was ruined.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: By the time he next ran into her, the pig had lost close to 10 pounds. They met at a museum benefit, a costume ball which he hosted, and which she hovered on the edges of, guzzling rum punch and gathering quote she'd heard a 1,000 times before. "Wonderful party and, of course, it's for such a good cause."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The parrot was, she liked to joke, back with the living, by which I mean section, not the sensation of being alive. She'd assumed that the pig would be in disguise, and was surprised to see him in the same dark suit he worn at the restaurant. He was standing at the bar, nursing a glass of water.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: And she came from behind and tapped him on the shoulder. "Let me guess," she said, "you're Henry Bacon, right?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Who's he?" the pig asked.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The parrot rolled her eyes. "American architect, designed a little something called the Lincoln Memorial?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Oh," the the pig said, "that Henry Bacon." He was going to admit that he was no one or, at least, no one special, when the parrot stepped back and examined him again over the rim of her punch class.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "I've got it," she said, "you're Luther Ham, took the silver medal for 200 meter freestyle, Helsinki 1952. Little wisp of a thing, but, boy, did he have shoulders."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Right," the pig said. "So who are you supposed to be?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The parrot shrugged and held up her glass for a refill. "I thought I'd go all out and come as a two-bit journalist." For verification, she presented an ink stained claw. "So hey," she added, "I'm sorry about that article."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "That's all right," the pig told her.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "All right for you," the parrot said, "I'm the one with the god damn hawk calling me every 10 minutes. Now he wants to go after Middle Easterners. Heard of a Persian cat who runs a parking garage down by the civic center and is after me to write an expose."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: The pig laughed for the first time in months, and immediately thereafter, as was his habit, he began to analyze why. Was it the idea of this parrot bedeviled by a ridiculous hawk, or the image of a long-haired cat making change in one of those sweltering little booths? He pondered this for days but never reached a satisfying conclusion.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Earth to pig, Earth to pig," the parrot said.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: And he looked down to see her wing resting on his stomach.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "Is it my imagination or have you lost some weight?"

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "No," he told her, "I mean, yes I did. It's not your imagination." He thought of how kind it was for her to mention it. And then he noticed how oddly satisfying it felt to be patted down by a wing.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: Meanwhile, the parrot was still talking. "Don't get me wrong," she said, "I have seen a cockatoo in my time, but I'm not dating anyone now if that's what you're wondering." She grabbed a passing appetizer, dumped the caviar back onto the tray and ate only the cracker. "A cliche, I know, parrot eats a cracker, but fish eggs make me bloat."

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: "It's the salt," the pig told her . He'd hoped to say something more interesting, but, just then, the band started up. A wolf, in sheep's clothing, called out for a foxtrot. And as if a switch had been thrown, the party came to life. Here was the hare in cat's pajamas dancing with a chameleon whose costume changed with every turn. The Ugly Duckling cut in on a swan. A trio of mice lowered their sunglasses, and as they scouted the floor for partners, the parrot turned to the pig and held out her claw.

segments.speaker: David  Sedaris
segments.text: He accepted it awkwardly in his hoof, this spindly pitchfork, this warm, mottled twig. And so began, what the reporter would later refer to, as her days of swine and roses.
